'''''Persicaria maculosa''''' (syn. ''Polygonum persicaria'') is an [[annual plant]] in the [[Polygonaceae|buckwheat family]], [[Polygonaceae]]. Common names include '''lady's thumb''',<ref>{{ITIS| id = 20915 | taxon = ''Polygonum persicaria''| accessdate = 15 October 2007}}</ref> '''spotted lady's thumb''', '''Jesusplant''', and '''redshank'''.<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |accessdate=2016-08-16 }}</ref><ref name=grin>{{GRIN | accessdate = 2017-12-18}}</ref> It is widespread across Eurasia from Iceland south to Portugal and east to Japan.<ref>[http://luirig.altervista.org/flora/taxa/index1.php?scientific-name=persicaria+maculosa Altervista Flora Italiana, ''Persicaria maculosa'' Gray] includes photos and European distribution map</ref><ref name=jing>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=220010832 Flora of China, ''Polygonum persicaria'' Linnaeus, 1753.  <big>蓼</big> liao ]</ref> It is also present as an [[introduced species|introduced]] and [[invasive species]] in North America, where it was first noted in the [[Great Lakes]] region in 1843 and has now spread through most of the continent.<ref>{{cite web |title= List of invasive species in the Great Lakes Great Lakes United / Union Saint-Laurent Grands Lacs |url= http://www.glu.org/en/node/199 |access-date= 2009-02-07 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20090429205753/http://www.glu.org/en/node/199 |archive-date= 2009-04-29 }}</ref><ref name=NatureServe/><ref>[http://bonap.net/MapGallery/State/Persicaria%20maculosa.png Biota of North America Program 2014 state-level distribution map]</ref>

==Description==
''Persicaria maculosa'' is an annual herb up to {{convert|1|m}} tall,<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last1=Elias|first1=Thomas S.|title=Edible Wild Plants: A North American Field Guide to Over 200 Natural Foods|last2=Dykeman|first2=Peter A.|publisher=[[Sterling Publishing|Sterling]]|year=2009|isbn=978-1-4027-6715-9|location=New York|page=110|oclc=244766414|orig-date=1982}}</ref> with an erect, rather floppy stem with swollen joints. The leaves are alternate and almost stalkless. The leaf blades often have a brown or black spot in the centre and are narrowly ovate and have entire margins. Each leaf base has stipules which are fused into a stem-enclosing sheath that is loose and fringed with long hairs at the upper end. The [[inflorescence]] is a dense spike. The perianth of each tiny pink flower consists of four or five lobes, fused near the base. There are six stamens, two fused carpels and two styles. The fruit is a shiny black, three-edged [[achene]]. This plant flowers from July to September in the temperate Northern Hemisphere.<ref name=jing/><ref name=NatureGate>{{cite web|url=http://www.luontoportti.com/suomi/en/kukkakasvit/redshank |title=Redshank: ''Persicaria maculosa'' |publisher=NatureGate |access-date=2013-12-30}}</ref><ref>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=220010181 Flora of North America, ''Persicaria maculosa'' Gray, 1821. Spotted lady's-thumb, redshank, renouée persicaire ]</ref>

==Taxonomy==
The species was first described, as ''Polygonum persicaria'', by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1753.<ref name=IPNI_696241-1/> It was first successfully transferred to the genus ''[[Persicaria]]'' by [[Samuel Frederick Gray]] in 1821, under the name ''Persicaria maculosa''.<ref name=IPNI_206340-2/> The name "''Persicaria persicaria''" cannot be used because [[tautonym]]s – binomial names that use the same word for both the genus and the species epithet – are prohibited by the [[International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants]], and a replacement name (''[[nomen novum]]'') must be used.<ref>[http://www.iapt-taxon.org/nomen/main.php?page=art23 International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants (Melbourne Code)] see section 23.4</ref> For this reason the transfer of the species to ''Persicaria'' by [[John Kunkel Small]] in 1903, which used the tautonym, is invalid.<ref name=IPNI_190848-2/>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Persicaria maculosa'' is native to [[Europe]] and [[Asia]], where it can be mistaken for ''[[Polygonum minus]]''. The latter has narrower leaves, usually less than 1 cm wide. It has been introduced to [[North America]] and is naturalised throughout the mainland continent,<ref>[https://plants.usda.gov/java/nameSearch?keywordquery=Persicaria+maculosa&mode=sciname&submit.x=0&submit.y=0 USDA]</ref> growing along roadsides, riverbanks, and on fallow ground. In the United States, it is very similar to [[Polygonum pensylvanicum|Pennsylvania smartweed]], but redshank has a fringe of hairs at the top of the [[ochrea]], something which Pennsylvania smartweed lacks. The species has also been found in New Zealand and Australia.<ref>[http://bie.ala.org.au/species/urn:lsid:biodiversity.org.au:apni.taxon:387589# Atlas of Living Australia,  ''Persicaria maculosa'' Gray, Jesus Plant]</ref><ref>[http://www.iucnredlist.org/details/175559/0 IUCN Red List of Threatened Species, ''Persicaria maculosa'']</ref>

==Ecology==
In the British Isles, this plant is a weed, without natural habitat, and always associated with human activity.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Simmonds|first=N W|title=Biological flora of the British Isles. ''Polygonum'' L|journal=Journal of Ecology|volume=33|year=1945|issue=33|pages=117–143| doi = 10.2307/2256567|jstor=2256567}}</ref> It likes moist soils, particularly rich ones, and [[peat|acid peaty]] [[loams]].<ref>{{cite journal|last=Long|first=H. C.|title=Weeds of arable land|journal=MAFF Bulletin|year=1938|issue=108}}</ref> It does not like lime, and [[Liming (soil)|liming]] is cited as a means to fight it.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Fenton|first=E. W.|title=Poisonous and milk-staining plants|journal=Pamphlet of Edinburgh and East of Scotland College of Agriculture|year=1931|series=New series|issue=4|pages=7–31}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=Bond|first=W.|title=The biology and non chemical control of Redshank (''Persicaria maculosa'' Gray)|url=http://www.gardenorganic.org.uk/organicweeds/|publisher=HDRA|access-date=13 October 2013}}</ref>

==Cultivation and uses==
''Persicaria maculosa'' contains [[persicarin]] and [[tannin]]s. The young leaves may be eaten as a [[leaf vegetable]].<ref name=":0" /> It is often seen as a weed and rarely cultivated. A yellow dye can be produced from this plant with [[alum]] used as a [[mordant]].
